posts.body_html:
Didn't grow a veggie garden this summer due to the drought, but with food prices soaring and a professional background in growing, it was illogical NOT to grow a winter garden, so here's the crops! Pics taken 11/9/22:

When it comes to broccoli and brussel sprouts, don't grow that open pollinated seeds unless you have the absolute perfect conditions where it doesn't get too cold or too warm EVER! I started these brussel sprouts in August I think, and looks like they're finally starting to sprout up! this is Jade Cross E F-1:


come on baby, sprout up! Just need a few more weeks before I can roast these puppies!


Here is emerald Jewel F1 Broccoli, my favorite looking one! I think I gave these plants too much chicken Dew-dew: the plants got enormous, but the heads are just average sized this year:




Some purple broccoli in the background. I crossed a select individual of early purple sprouting (which had a nice sized head) with burgundy in the hopes of getting burgundy like offspring (eg. quick and easy to flower, needs no cold snap to bloom, large heads, short, compact plants). Unfortunately, all of the offspring are like burgundy (needs cold to bloom, probably will produce smaller heads) so I've started another batch and will back cross it to Burgundy again in hopes of getting a few seedlings that will be like burgundy! BTW, burgundy is male sterile, so there's no way to produce seeds with it unless you outcross it to something else:

posts.body_html:
Got down to 25F last night, here are some frozen veggies in the garden! Pics taken 12/2/22:
Napa cabbage, emiko hybrid f1:


The last of the first batch of broccoli, this is emerald jewel F1. Started off super small, but over time, it reached a decent size, this is one of the smaller ones from the batch:


Frozen! I guess the cold never bothered it anyways, da-da-da-daaaah! For those of you without kids, that's a reference to the movie frozen....



My experimental purple broccoli, burgundy x early purple sprouting. These plants are monster sized and there is some broccoli heads forming, finally! Started these I think end of July:


Ice, ice, baby!


Asparagus bed pretty much dormant, I'll take those old tops off once they turn brown. These were started in June 2021, and I've been harvesting them throughout the season. Next spring should have a nice yield. This is Connover's collosal and Precoce de Argenteuil. I've been slowly culling the females because many of them were completely LOADED with fruit (they set seeds like crazy, can overcrowd the bed with seedlings, and have lower yields compared to the males since the energy goes into seed production), but man, there's a lot of them and I'm wondering if that was the right thing to do:


Frozen butter lettuce, unscathed! Hours later, you couldn't tell this was frozen:



Giant fronds of purple passion asparagus some were over 6' tall this season! These turned out to be hermaphrodites and do set a small amount of seeds, but I ain't cullin them!


super sugar snap peas. I covered these last night. If you don't the tips will burn from the freeze and it'll slow down production:


Turnips, this one is Mikado F1:


Celery can withstand some level of freezing, but only to a point. it'll eventually get damaged if it freezes hard several days in a row. This time around, they're totally fine:


Frozen cilantro volunteer, freeze resistant to a point:


Baby carrots! These don't like the freeze and the leaves tend to turn purple from cold stress if this happens too often:

posts.body_html:
So here's an update on the Burgundy x early purple sprouting broccoli, turned out really nice! The plants aren't uniform and there are definitely ones with big heads, versus ones with lots of little side shoots that form a decent sized head. NEvertheless, they all taste great and have a much better yield than early purple sprouting, so it's an improvement, but burgundy is superior in head size. However, unlike burgundy, these do require cool temperatures in order to initiate flowering, I started them in late July 2022! we've been harvesting these since a week before christmas, so it's really nice because the crop doesn't all come in at once. There are still a few plants that are 2-3 weeks away from harvesting, so in that sense, this cross is far superior to the others if you want staggered food production.

Once you harvest the main head, the plant can still produce side shoots, which lengthens the harvest period even more! I'm guessing there will be up to a 2 month harvest period for this cross!

Burgundy x early purple sprouting, pics taken January 2023:

This is a nice individual with a decent sized head and lots of side shoots:


Same exact plant, zoomed out. Looks small from this perspective:


a different plant. the florets look small from this angle but look at how big the plant is! They're actually decent sized:


Here's another individual, absolute joy growing these!

posts.body_html:
It was unseasonably cool this spring: we successfully produced broccoli in July! Usually, it fails when it gets too hot and buttons or forms very tiny heads. Here's a little updated tour of the veggie garden:





These heads were enormous! This variety is pacman, harvested only a few days ago, taste is superb and surprisingly sweet!


some purple cauliflower, also harvested in July!


Pretty sure this is emerald jewel, also consistently does well here:


New Red Fire loose leaf lettuce from Botanical interests (photographed July 19th, 2023): if you want to grow lettuce, this is the one, produces all year round and didn't bolt even though it was in the high 90's while it was growing! I got some from Harris seeds and the leaves were extremely bitter, their strain wasn't as good as botanical interests:



Cucurbita maxima 'sweet meat' aka winter squash. Almightydolla from the Sarracenia forum aka Steve Galic recommended this strain, it grows long vines like a pumpkin and needs quite a bit of space. Super fun to grow so far:


Something I've never tried growing before: kabocha squash! This is sweet mama F1, produces far more female flowers than male flowers. semi bush, and so far it's an absolute joy to grow:


about a week and a half after being pollinated:


Honey select corn. If you've been skunked by corn (eg. they don't taste good), this is the variety to try! 75% SH2, 25% SE. Doesn't require isolation from other varieties to produce sweet kernels, which is one reason sweet corn comes out starchy!


Benny's eyes are absolutely hilarious! You can see the size of the kabocha squash plants, they're actually pretty enormous! There's only 5 plants there! (center, background) Looks like they'll be very productive too! To the right, there are 3-4 Astia zucchini squash: this variety produces small plants but pushes out tons of squash so long as you keep harvesting them. Highly recommended! To the far left/background is the viney sweet Meat:

posts.body_html:
jgreen1025: you're welcome! Glad to hear you're enjoying the photos and stories!

Regarding Zucchini, I highly recommend trying the variety I'm growing called Astia, it's from Renee's Garden. In the last picture above, they're the plants to the very right: there are 4 plants and notice the plant size at maturity: they're small and compact. Despite the small size, they produce the same amount as a regular sized Zucchini! They produce more female than male flowers, which helps direct energy into fruit rather than leaf production. It helps if your neighbors are growing squash, or if you have other squash varieties nearby, or grow 3-4 plants. 4 plants is probably enough for 4-6 people, although my wife and I eat veggies like crazy and we're able to keep up with 4 zucchini plants. I hand pollinate them all, which means almost every single female flower produces fruit. They need to be harvested constantly if you want maximum production, otherwise they'll just produce 1-2 large fruit and stop growing. Every week, we harvest about 5-6 zucchini from those 4 plants!

FWIW, both botanical interests and Renee's Garden consistently have high quality genetics from my experience, I highly recommend them, their quality is on par if not better than Johnny's seeds, which occasionally isn't great.

posts.body_html:
Given the locally high prices of fresh produce in my area (probably near or at the highest in the nation), we grew 100% of all of our produce for several months this year. At one point, an approximate 40% of my daily food intake came directly from the garden! We grew everything that you can grow in our climate.

I also went a little crazy with some squash breeding experiments, did a pretty decent sized population grow out to select the best individuals for some crosses:


Mottled thai pumpkin:


mostly candystick delicata:


the green ones here are sweet mama F1, this is the best kabocha squash in terms of flavor, that I've been able to find so far:


guatemalan green ayote. Yes, the flesh is green and no, it's not rotting!






The guatemalan green ayote is super beautiful on the outside too!


A neighbor asked me recently if we're growing in full force for the winter, the answer is nope. I have to go back and rely on the stores: without a greenhouse or hoop houses, it's too cold and the days are too short to get significant production in my climate during the winter. For now, we're supplemented with brassicas and winter greens:


Rommanesco, these literally go for $5/head, and the ones at the store are about half the size as this one!


incredible amount of leaf biomass is needed to create a decent sized romanesco inflorescence:


Marte Brussel Sprouts, perhaps the most success I've had so far with brussel sprouts. You want to start these in late june/early July. I actually want to try starting them in early June, they always seem to ripen in December rather than October or November:


Saijo persimmon. Acquired this tree as a tiny seedling in 2007, it was $55! It struggled and never grew much until I bought my house and planted it into sandy loam. IT didn't like growing in toxic serpentine soil. Anyways, Within 4 years, it went from a stunted, barely alive stick to a full blown producing tree! Unusual Persimmon varieties in CA are near impossible to acquire: almost nobody locally produces trees, and nobody in the rest of the US will ship them here due to quarantine rules:

posts.body_html:
not much going on with Sarracenia just yet, but there's a little bit of activity in the veggie garden!


Guatemalan green ayote, still in good shape, this was photographed march 24, 2025, but it looks the same right now. The shelf life varies from plant to plant and the condition of the fruit when it was harvested, some last longer than others:


Finally swimming in asparagus for once in my life! Everytime in the past that I tried to grow asparagus, by the time it got big enough, I had to move!




doesn't look like much, but this bed has produced maybe 20 lbs so far this season and it's just getting started:


I've always struggled with garlic, and have tried many, many times. Yes, there have been years that they do well, but I haven't ever been able to harvest my garlic and use that as seed for the next fall, it always fails. I always have to go back to buying "seed garlic" to succeed again. This is the first year that I haven't had to buy seed garlic, these are from my own plants last season. Way too many details why I was failing, but in a nutshell it was due to overhead watering (caused rust outbreaks), soil got too wet during the rainy season, and too much nitrogen! I still get rust, which is something that is due to our cool, humid spring conditions, it happens to all growers here. Not sure how to manage that but rust doesn't overwinter on the bulbs. I exlcusively feed them with an organic tomato fertilizer (4-5-6 or something like that) and it has worked out very well! It's still an art, too much fertilizer and you'll get rot/all sorts of diseases:




Some big heads expected:


Neighbor drove by the other day and said "yo mike....looks like salinas over here!" My wife saw this and shook her head, saying "OMG, you even used black landscaping fabric..." She's concerned about the critters this patch will invite, so I started it pretty far from the house (I have more than an acre of land):


Never grown Strawberries before, not sure why. Maybe because of my poor childhood experience (my mom grew it when I was a kid, the strawberries never tasted good (poor variety selection?). Hopefully these will be good, did a lot of homework before attempting it:

posts.body_html:
some updates on the strawberry patch. So far, the biggest challenge is how to keep the raccoons out! They'll get in there and eat EVERY LAST one of them! I have bird netting on top and that is a game changer, the blue jays haven't had a single chance. The deer have found weakpoints here and there with the netting and got a few leaves, but for the most part, they can't get in either. But when you have smart animals that know how to sneak their way in, it's a struggle.

Nevertheless, overall, this strawberry patch has been a success, although the fruit production is relatively low. This is because I mixed in about 2 wheel barrels full of horse manure compost per row when prepping the beds, which means too much nitrogen. I thought by now the N would all be used up, but guess not: you want to get the plants to size up first and then switch them into flower mode. When you have too much N, it gives you great growth with zero flowering! Here's what I found from this "experiment":
Albion: super nitrogen sensitive, the whole bed hasn't produced anything after the first flush of flowering, which I pinched. Produces enormous numbers of runners: the one plant that I didn't pinch off the runners is producing flowers, so maybe that's one way to offset high nitrogen.
seascape: doesn't care, producing anyways!
sequoia: doesn't care, producing anyways, but super small, rosetted plants that haven't sent any runners.
Fort Laramie:doesn't care, producing like crazy anyways!
Mara Des Bois: doesn't care, producing but this is a low vigor, low producer
Carolina white: produced a ton of runners, didn't pinch any since only one plant survived, flowering now.
Monterey: super nitrogen sensitive, huge plant, no fruit
Cabrillo: super nitrogen sensitive, but one plant was allowed to runner like crazy and it looks like it's going to flower now...finally!
Hood: unknown, just planted a few days ago! I for sure didn't mix in any high nitrogen compost in this bed!

Seascape: this was a nice sized one, and I was going to leave it on the vine for 2 more days, but the raccoons got it:


some more seascape. In my climate (northern california), this is a great producer and they taste great, but you have to leave them on the plant for a good day or two after they turn totally red otherwise they won't be sweet. In warmer climates, they're probably sweet at this stage:




The beds. The row in the foreground is albion, the plants look incredible! Keep in mind, they were planted in February and it's May, they sized up quickly! All plant but zero berries...I leached them out this morning with heavy overhead watering and gave them high organic P,K, so hopefully that will help trigger them to switch into flower mode. If they do flower, the berries will likely be pretty darn big:




Seascape. This plant has tall, long petioles:

Cabrillo: super nitrogen sensitive, but one plant was allowed to runner like crazy and it looks like it's going to flower now...finally!
Hood: unknown, just planted a few days ago!  I for sure didn't mix in any high nitrogen compost in this bed!
Seascape: this was a nice sized one, and I was going to leave it on the vine for 2 more days, but the raccoons got it:
some more seascape.  In my climate (northern california), this is a great producer and they taste great, but you have to leave them on the plant for a good day or two after they turn totally red otherwise they won't be sweet.  In warmer climates, they're probably sweet at this stage:
The beds.  The row in the foreground is albion, the plants look incredible!  Keep in mind, they were planted in February and it's May, they sized up quickly!  All plant but zero berries...I leached them out this morning with heavy overhead watering and gave them high organic P,K, so hopefully that will help trigger them to switch into flower mode.  If they do flower, the berries will likely be pretty darn big:
Seascape.  This plant has tall, long petioles:

Depending on where you are located will determine when to start brussels sprouts. If you're by the California coast, early spring will give you an early fall harvest, early to mid summer planting will yield a winter harvest. As mentioned above, no matter what you do, stick with hybrids, as they are far more successful than open pollinated varieties. I always failed with OP brussel sprouts but have had consistent results with hybrids. The patch at night, photos taken 11/5/25:


During the day! Franklin F1 Brussels sprouts in the foreground and redarling F1 in the background:


Redarling F1 close up, it takes a very long time! These were started in June 2025 and it's already middle of November, still no sprouts to harvest!


On the other hand, Marte F1, planted at the same time as Redarling F1, is almost ready to pick, maybe another week or two left:


Franklin is maybe 3-4 weeks away. Nice thing is you can start 3 different varieties all with different finishing times, at the same time, as an example, and have them ready at 3 different times, so you end up with a constant harvest over many months:

If you've never struggled with garlic, consider yourself lucky!

okay, an update on garlic being grown here in zone 9, Northern California. It stopped raining significantly for over a month and the garlic beds that weren't planted on a hill appear to be recovering well from temporary flooding due to heavy rains. It's pretty tricky because last year, the garlic did very well without being grown in hills , but perhaps that specific spot drained better than the spots that were chosen this year.

Unfortunately, we have a forecast for 10 days of rain, much of which will be heavy rain. Will this second rain event be the nail in the coffin for the beds not on hills?

First off, California Early (softneck). This proven strain does well in our climate year after year, and the plants are looking exceptional this season. About 2 years ago, one of the beds had very yellow lower leaves early in the season, likely due to temporary waterlogging, but then they recovered. The plants seen below came from those!


The only challenge with growing on this hill is gophers: when the rest of the field gets flooded, they all congregate here! In less than 24 hours, a single gopher ate 3 plants! From experience: Without trapping them, this entire bed would be gone by the end of the season, gophers are exeptionally notorious in my area:


Another bed: it took me 3 days to catch the gopher that attacked this bed, look at how much went missing (foreground)! Plants stressed from earlier waterlogging, but recovering in this photo:



Lorz Italian, recovering well from temporary waterlogging:



Chesnok Red. Barely started growing and got really stressed from waterlogging. Sort of recovering, but doesn't look great:


California early (smaller plants, foreground), Inchelium red (bigger plants, background). This spot didn't flood as bad:


Purple Glazer doing very well so far:



Northern Italian (softneck)recovering well from earlier waterlogging:


Rose Du Lautrec. These came from small bulbs, it's all I could get. They did recover from the first flooding event but they overall don't look great right now:



Music to the left and Native Creole to the right. Notice all the lower yellowing leaves from flooding: these got set back pretty hard, but the new growth is healthy:


this bed overall looks the worst. It was planted the latest (sometime in November) and just as the plants emerged they got stunted from flooding. They are recovering but I'm nervous about this next rain taking them out! In this bed (foreground to background): German Red, Rose Du Lautrec, Chesnok Red, and Spanish Roja (3 rows in the background). I'm sad about the spanish roja, it started off so strong in the beginning!

Strawberries are starting to wake up! I have one bed of june bearing strawberries just for fun, they were started last May and this winter, I cut them all to the ground. June Bearers need that winter dormancy to produce their one flush of fruit, which usually happens around June (this is different than day neutral strawberries, which flower and produce fruit as long as the weather is favorable. They stop producing from about late November until about late March/early april for me).

On the left is Mary's Peak (which we call Mary's Pizzle), a relatively new, patented variety that was released in 2018. I think I read somewhere it's the "replacement" for hood strawberries. The row on the right is the famous Hood Strawberry (released in 1965). Mary's peak is super vigorous, seems quite disease resistant, and is overall easy to grow whereas hood is notorious for being susceptible to diseases, especially viruses, and is overall more challenging to cultivate. That said, hood is known for its flavor....I guess we'll see about that!


The hood strawberry plants have multiple growth points and are probably gonna produce heavy! Prior to cleaning this up, there were HUNDREDS of runners! In retrospect, I probably should have grown these with straw instead of landscaping fabric: june bearers will give you the best yield with a ton of plants, whereas day neutrals really need their space to produce well:


We have 5 beds of strawberries this year. We went really big this year because last year with 3 productive beds (the 4th was the june bearers, which need a full year to produce, and the fifth was started late last season), we only got over abundance around the fall. Maybe this year, with the june bearers producing for their first time, there will be a good amount all season long:


This is what I had for lunch the other day, some tender asparagus shoots! The bed will be harvestable every 2-3 days for maybe 2 months starting now-ish. It's really worth having your own asparagus plot, seeds are the most economical way to get them going:
